The argument presented in the text is logically incoherent and structurally flawed due to a complete disconnect between its premise and its conclusion.

First, the text begins with a factual question ("what is the name of the planet humans live on?") which is entirely unrelated to the subsequent argument. This creates an immediate logical break, as the answer to the question (Earth) has no bearing on the claim regarding workweeks.

Second, the core argument—that implementing a four-day workweek will increase employee satisfaction—is supported by evidence citing increased productivity and decreased staff turnover. While these are positive outcomes, they are not direct evidence of "employee satisfaction." Productivity and retention are distinct metrics that may correlate with satisfaction but do not definitively prove it. An employee might stay in a job due to lack of alternatives (low turnover) or work harder under pressure (high productivity) without necessarily being more satisfied. Therefore, the reasoning contains a logical gap by equating operational benefits with subjective well-being.

Finally, the argument relies on anecdotal or generalized evidence ("Companies abroad... report") without specifying which companies, the scale of the tests, or the methodology used. This lack of specific, verifiable data weakens the evidentiary support.

In summary, the argument is weak because it is disjointed (starting with an irrelevant question), relies on proxy metrics for its main claim (using productivity/turnover to prove satisfaction), and lacks specific, rigorous evidence to support its generalization.
